title: Heat is not temperature
target: Distinguish temperature from energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
criteria: Identify the direction of spontaneous heat transfer.
Explain why amount and material matter.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: Two samples of the same material are at the same temperature, but one has three times the mass. Which claim is best?
options: Equal temperature does not mean equal total thermal energy.
The smaller sample must contain no particle motion.
The larger sample must have a higher temperature.
Equal temperature guarantees equal total thermal energy.
cpa.guide: Temperature is an intensive measure; the amount of material affects total internal energy.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: A thermometer reads 45°C. What does this reading directly describe?
options: The number of particles in the sample.
Heat flow in joules per second.
The total energy of any object at that reading.
Temperature, not an amount of heat in joules.
cpa.guide: Temperature alone does not specify total energy or heat transfer.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: A 48°C ceramic tile contacts a 16°C metal block. Initially, which way is spontaneous net heat transfer?
options: Toward whichever object is heavier, regardless of temperature.
From tile to block.
Both transfer directions have equal net energy immediately.
From block to tile.
cpa.guide: Net heat transfer is initially from hotter to colder, independent of which material is metal.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: Two objects are in thermal equilibrium. What statement follows?
options: They must contain equal total energy.
They must have equal masses.
All microscopic motion stops.
There is no net heat transfer due to a temperature difference.
cpa.guide: Thermal equilibrium means equal temperature and no temperature-driven net heat flow.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: Equal masses of two materials receive equal energy with no loss or phase change. Their temperature rises differ. What property can explain the difference?
options: One temperature rise must be invented.
Heat must always change mass instead.
Different specific heats.
Different definitions of a joule.
cpa.guide: ΔT = Q/(mc); with equal Q and m, a different c changes the rise.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

cpa.prompt: A cup and a tank contain the same liquid at 50°C. Both cool to 30°C with no phase change. Which releases more energy if the tank holds much more liquid?
options: They release equal energy because initial temperatures match.
Neither can transfer energy below 50°C.
The tank, because more mass undergoes the same temperature change.
The cup, because small objects always contain more heat.
cpa.guide: For the same material and ΔT, |Q| is proportional to mass.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.
